text: In God's name, the Compassionate, the Merciful.
Praise be to God, Lord of all worlds.

Peace and blessings upon the noblest of God's
creation,

our Prophet Muhammad, his family, companions, and
followers until the Day of Judgment.

Today, God willing, I will discuss the Holy Quran
and

the author's fingerprint: how we can use it to
distinguish

between different writers. Let me begin by recalling
that when a messenger is sent,
God, exalted be He, sends him with two things:
a miracle showing that he is a messenger from God,
and the teachings he must convey to God's servants.
Moses had his staff,

and the Torah. Jesus healed those born blind and
those with leprosy,
and he also had the Gospel.

For the Prophet, peace be upon him, the miracle and
the teachings are one and the same.
The Holy Quran is the miracle.

The Quran itself challenged the Arabs to produce a
surah like it.
God says: 'If you doubt what We have revealed

to Our servant, produce a surah like it, and call
your witnesses besides God,

if you are truthful.' Another verse says: 'Or do
they say

he invented it? Say: Then produce ten invented
surahs like it,

and call whoever you can besides God, if you are
truthful.'

Another verse says: 'If humans and jinn joined
together to produce

the like of this Quran, they could not, even if they
helped one another.'

Now let us move straight to the content of this
presentation.

I'll briefly introduce the author's fingerprint and
how
we can extract it from different texts.
We can use it to group texts automatically
by their author's fingerprint, or by the time
or period in which they were written.
After this introduction, I'll move to an experiment
with prose: an experiment involving ten authors.

Then I'll move to the experiment with the Holy Quran
and Arabic poetry.
I'll finish with a conclusion and the findings.

Stylometry, or computational stylistics, as we might
call it,
is a technique we can use on a computer
to identify an author's fingerprint.
It can also identify the different periods or times
when these works were written,
whether poetry or prose.
This algorithm uses hierarchical clustering.
It extracts the most frequent words from the texts,

because these are used in different kinds of
writing,
regardless of the subject.

The same writer uses the same prepositions,
conjunctions, and similar words
when writing two different texts:
one about economics and another about politics.
These words form

the mathematical vector that represents the author's
fingerprint.

We then use established distance measures to group
the texts
into clusters based on similarities in their writing
style. These algorithms treat a text
as a mathematical vector.
For example, the blue vector in this diagram
is represented in three dimensions.

In the same way, we generate mathematical vectors
for all the texts,

with 100 dimensions. These vectors come from the
most

frequent words in the corpus: the collection of
texts being analyzed.
For example, here are the vectors generated
for the texts labeled H1 and onward.

The algorithm measures the distances between the
generated vectors,
and merges the closest ones.
Then
it merges entire groups according to similarity.
A different or outlying text, such as J1,
ends up in a different cluster.
This is a very important experiment:
the experiment with ten travelers.
We used ten different books,
by writers who lived at roughly the same time,
and wrote about the same subject.
We wanted to see whether we could use

the most frequent words to distinguish between these
different writings.
We took about ten samples from each book.
The samples were selected randomly.
So, from each book,
we had passages from the start, the end,
and the middle. Each sample was preprocessed so that
the final comparison used specific features,
whether letters or words:
the same words occurring in the different samples.

On that basis, we carried out the comparison between
the vectors.

generated from these samples. In the first
experiment, we found that

the clusters were unclear, and the samples had been
grouped

incorrectly, because the text passages were very
short.
We used about 500 words or fewer from each author.
As you can see, the clusters were unclear. But in

the second experiment, we increased the word count
until
each sample had about 2,000 words.
The clustering then looked different.

As you can see, the clusters became very clear: the
texts grouped by

author. This shows that it is possible to group
different
writings by author using the words
that occur most frequently.

The second experiment is the most important to me,
and the subject of this presentation:
comparing the Holy Quran with Arabic poetry.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, was accused of being
a poet.

The challenge was to produce something like this
Quran,
and they failed to do so.

They composed metrical verse, rhyming poetry, and so
on,
but could not produce anything resembling the Quran.
For this experiment, we collected poetry from the
Pre-Islamic period to the Modern period.
A very large collection, or corpus,

so that we could compare these texts with the Holy
Quran.
As you can see here,
the corpus covers various periods, from Pre-Islamic,

Early Islamic, Umayyad, Abbasid, Andalusian,
Ayyubid, Fatimid, and Mamluk,
to Ottoman and Modern.

We collected these groups of poems by different
writers.
The corpus contained approximately
ten million words,
nearly six million lines of poetry,

by around a thousand poets from different historical
periods.
The first result, when we used the complete texts,
was that, as you can see, there are two clusters.
One contains the Holy Quran alone.

The other, on the right, contains all the poetry
from the different periods.

You can see that Umayyad poetry resembles
Pre-Islamic poetry,
and these, in turn, resemble Early Islamic poetry.
The other periods then group into different

clusters. The Holy Quran is clearly distinct from
these texts.
Then, when we took samples,
we took samples from each period.
The result was, again, that all

ten samples from the Holy Quran clustered on their
own on the left.
The remaining poetry clustered on the right.

There is another very important point I'd like to
draw attention to:

the ten Pre-Islamic poetry samples clustered close
to

the Umayyad period, but still formed their own
group.
This means they have distinctive characteristics.
This proves that there really is Pre-Islamic poetry,
contrary to what Professor Taha Hussein said.

This issue should therefore be studied
scientifically.

We should identify the features: the words, letters,
or
the model used,
on which this diagram was based,
and which indicated that Pre-Islamic poetry has...

distinctive features that set it apart from the
other periods.
The important question, then, is:
if we want to identify the features,
the words used in these models and diagrams

that distinguish the Quran from the other texts, and
study them,
yes, we can do that, but using
other methods.
PCA is
the subject of the next slide.
With PCA, what we are trying to do is...
Previously, we examined a text through the hundred

words forming its vector, measuring its distance
from the other vectors.

Now we want to look at these texts in just two
dimensions.
That is why we use this technique.
There are groups of words which

occur more often in one group of texts and less
often in the other,

according to the clusters. Here, for example, we
have the Quran on

the left, surrounded by some of its distinguishing
words.

On the right are the other poems and the words that
distinguish them.

Some words are clear: for example, 'Allah' ('God'),
on the left beside the Quran.
And 'al-dahr' ('time').

These are clear. But other words, such as
demonstratives and so on,

need input and analysis from language specialists to
understand

why they occur more here than in the other texts,
and distinguish the Quran.
If we move to two-word sequences,

we again find different expressions in phrases or
pairs of words.

The Holy Quran consistently differs in its
expressions,
its words, and its vocabulary.

If we leave that analysis and move to sequences of
letters,
starting with single letters, for example,
this is a result I think is very important.
We find that a number of letters appear
on the Quran's side
more than in the poetry.
The Quran used these letters more often.
I don't know why. Perhaps it comes from vocabulary

containing words that had been little used, or were
unique to it.
They did not appear even in the later periods.
It was distinguished by these letters.
For example,
here is a comparison,
just to enlarge the picture,

between the Quran, Umayyad, Early Islamic, and
Abbasid poetry. These are the same

letters that distinguished it from all the other
periods:
mim, kaf, nun, ha, and dhal.
I don't know the explanation.
We need language specialists
to give us,
as they say,
an informed scholarly opinion.
Likewise, if we use two letters,
splitting the text into sequences

of two letters, we again find the Quran distinct and
unique.
If we move to three letters,
we again find a different pattern.

If we move to seven letters, there is something to
discuss here.

I noticed that prepositions attach to nouns more
often in

the Quran. But in Pre-Islamic poetry, as I'll show
on
the next slide, they were very rare. What appeared

more often, however, was prepositions with the
particle, or
the definite article 'al-'.
These appeared frequently in the Quran.

I think the Quran then changed the way the language
was used, because other
poetry began using them.

Over time, it clearly began using prepositions
attached to 'al-'.

There is a view that, previously, prepositions did
not
attach directly to nouns in this way.

The noun took the genitive, as in 'jamil al-wajh'
('beautiful of face').
'Beautiful of face.'
Or, as the poet said:
'Whatever faults I may have,
my dog is timid and my camel calf is lean.'

The point is that the construction used to come like
this.
This is one result that may support that view.

But we also need scientific and technical analysis
from language
specialists. This should be put to them for further
discussion. In conclusion,

the Holy Quran's style is completely different from
poetry.
It cannot be poetry in any way.
It differs in every characteristic,
every feature, whether letters or words,
or what we call parts or sequences of letters:
two or three letters, and so on.

The Quran's style is completely different from the
various poetic
texts. And the Quran itself...

The Quran itself says in Surah Ya-Sin: 'We have not
taught him poetry,

nor is it fitting for him. It is only a reminder and
a clear Quran.'

It cannot be poetry. In al-Haqqah: 'It is not a
poet's speech; little do you believe.'

And in al-Shu'ara: 'Or do they say: a poet, for whom
we await the misfortunes of time?'
Let them wait until the Hour comes.
The Holy Quran will remain completely different,
from all poetry, all prose, and everything else.
It is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds.

May God bless our Prophet Muhammad, his family and
companions, and grant them peace.
Peace be upon you, and God's mercy and blessings.
